props.title: Period of Adjustment

sections.content: **Period of Adjustment** (1962) represents a fascinating pivot in Tennessee Williams adaptations, trading the playwright's typical southern Gothic intensity for lighter romantic comedy. Jane Fonda and Jim Hutton star as newlyweds struggling through early marriage, while Anthony Franciosa and Lois Nettleton play their friends dealing with their own marital crisis. The film marked George Roy Hill's directorial debut before he went on to helm classics like **Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid** (1969) and **The Sting** (1973). Unlike Williams' more famous screen adaptations like **A Streetcar Named Desire** (1951) or **Cat on a Hot Tin Roof** (1958), this gentler work explores marriage anxiety with a surprisingly modern sensibility.

sections.content: The early 1960s marked a transitional period for Hollywood's treatment of marriage and sexuality. While **Period of Adjustment** took a more comedic approach, films like **The Chapman Report** (1962) and **Two for the Seesaw** (1962) began exploring modern relationships with increasing frankness. This shift preceded the complete dissolution of the Production Code in 1968, which would allow for even more direct examinations of marriage and sexuality in films like **Bob & Carol & Ted & Alice** (1969). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Marriage in American Cinema

The film's exploration of newlywed anxiety created a template for later marriage-focused comedies. While **Period of Adjustment** maintains a relatively gentle tone, its honest portrayal of marital difficulties influenced everything from **The Four Seasons** (1981) to **When Harry Met Sally** (1989). The film's Christmas Eve setting also places it in an interesting subset of holiday films that use the season to examine relationship dynamics, similar to **The Apartment** (1960) and later works like **The Family Stone** (2005).
